summary:
ASTRA-MONITOR: AI-Powered Astronaut Health Monitoring System

ASTRA-MONITOR is a prototype designed to support astronaut health monitoring during space missions. It provides a centralized dashboard to display important health parameters, including heart rate, oxygen saturation, and body temperature. The system uses Normal, Warning, and Critical status indicators to make unusual readings easier to identify. Its smart analysis concept helps explain readings that fall outside expected ranges, while alerts highlight important changes that may require attention.

Our project addresses the challenge of monitoring astronaut health in space, where continuous observation and timely awareness of potential health concerns are essential. By combining health data visualization, anomaly detection concepts, and alert notifications, ASTRA-MONITOR aims to help mission-control teams make more informed decisions.

It is important because early awareness of unusual health patterns can support astronaut well-being and contribute to safer, more reliable space missions.
details:
Project Details

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

ASTRA-MONITOR is an AI-powered astronaut health monitoring and early-warning prototype designed to support astronaut well-being during space missions.

The system uses a Python-based virtual health data simulator to generate astronaut health readings, including heart rate, oxygen saturation (SpO₂), body temperature, and stress level. These readings are sent to a Java Spring Boot backend through REST APIs. The backend processes the data and stores it in a database. An AI/ML component analyzes health patterns, detects unusual readings, and estimates a risk level. The system can then generate alerts and send updates to the Mission Control dashboard.

The dashboard is designed to display astronaut status, health metrics, risk levels, alerts, and historical information[UNDER DEVELOPMENT] in an understandable format.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Helps mission-control teams monitor multiple astronauts from one dashboard.
  • Makes unusual health readings easier to identify through Normal, Warning, and Critical indicators.
  • Uses anomaly detection concepts to identify unusual patterns.
  • Provides explanations for detected abnormalities and highlights important alerts.
  • Creates a foundation for tracking health readings over time.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our intended impact is to improve awareness of astronaut health conditions during space missions. By combining data monitoring, anomaly detection, and alert notifications, ASTRA-MONITOR aims to support faster and more informed decisions by mission-control teams. In the future, it could be extended with validated medical reference data, improved predictive models, and real-time monitoring technologies.

4. What tools, programming languages, and software did we use?

  • Frontend: JavaScript, HTML, CSS.
  • Backend: Java 21, Spring Boot, Spring Web, and Maven.
  • AI/ML and simulator: Python, Scikit-learn, FastAPI, and Joblib.
  • Database: DBeaver.
  • Communication: REST APIs and WebSockets.
  • Development and collaboration: VS Code, IntelliJ IDEA, Git, GitHub, and Postmant

No physical health sensors were used in the prototype. Virtual sensor data is generated through a simulator.

5. How is the project creative?

The creative aspect of ASTRA-MONITOR is its combination of virtual health data simulation, AI-based anomaly detection, risk assessment, and a centralized Mission Control dashboard. Instead of displaying only raw numbers, the system aims to explain unusual patterns and highlight their importance through visual indicators and alerts. It also includes an interactive astronaut-focused interface to make health information easier to explore.

6. What factors did our team consider?

Our team considered:

  • The importance of continuous astronaut health monitoring.
  • The need for clear and understandable health information.
  • Early identification of unusual patterns.
  • Reliable data processing and storage.
  • Clear communication between the frontend, backend, and AI service.
  • Data validation and responsible use of health reference ranges.
  • Scalability for monitoring multiple astronauts.
  • The limitations of simulated data and the need for further testing before real-world use.
